abstract: Enterprise UX is the user experience (UX) design of software that organizations buy, roll out and govern: software as a service (SaaS) platforms, internal tools and artificial intelligence (AI) features used by many roles at once. ui-ux.agency, the design team of tkxel, designs enterprise UX for complex workflows, permissions, data-dense dashboards and design systems that hold up in security and accessibility reviews.
summary: Enterprise UX design for SaaS platforms, admin consoles and internal AI tools: role-based workflows, dense data screens and accessible design systems.
intro: IT and procurement approve enterprise software, while operators, analysts, approvers and admins use it all day. Our enterprise UX work designs for both groups, from the security review to the daily task.

challengesIntro: Enterprise UX is harder because six pressures stack up: many roles, dense data, security reviews, accessibility rules, AI features staff must trust and a legacy workflow to replace.

challenges.title: One product, many roles
challenges.body: The buyer is rarely the end user: IT, procurement and security approve the purchase, while admins, managers, operators, approvers and guests work in different modules. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) defines role-based access control (RBAC) as access authorizations attached to roles, not individuals, so each screen depends on the signed-in role.

challenges.title: Screens full of data
challenges.body: Operations teams filter a dashboard, then edit tables with dozens of columns and bulk actions. IBM Carbon Design System data tables offer sortable headers, expandable rows and batch actions. Salesforce's lightning-datatable, built on the Salesforce Lightning Design System blueprint, is not supported on mobile, so plan enterprise dashboard design desktop-first.

challenges.title: Security reviews before purchase
challenges.body: Enterprise buyers ask for a SOC 2 report, a System and Organization Controls attestation from an independent certified public accountant (CPA) firm. The firm tests controls against the American Institute of CPAs (AICPA) Trust Services Criteria, where security is required. Their security review then checks SSO, multi-factor authentication (MFA), role changes and the audit log.

challenges.title: Accessibility in the contract
challenges.body: Federal procurement follows the US Access Board's Revised Section 508 Standards, required since January 18, 2018, which incorporate WCAG 2.0 A and AA. Vendors document conformance in an Accessibility Conformance Report (ACR), usually built on the VPAT (Voluntary Product Accessibility Template). The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) Title II rule sets WCAG 2.1 AA for state and local government websites and apps.

challenges.title: AI features staff do not trust
challenges.body: The US Census Bureau reported in May 2026 that 37% of US firms with 250 or more employees were using AI. A wrong answer inside a finance or human resources approval flow costs more than in a consumer app, so staff need sources, human review and undo. Teams running several pilots can first pick the AI pilot worth taking to production.

challenges.title: Adoption after rollout
challenges.body: Power users build habits, shortcuts and saved views, and a changed interface wipes them out on launch day. Staff already juggle many tools: Okta's Businesses at Work 2025 report puts the 2024 global average at 101 apps per company. Adoption stalls when a rollout has no plan, and the help desk queue fills instead.

solutionsIntro: In enterprise software UX, we handle roles with a permission matrix, dense data with reusable table patterns and AI with review and approval steps, matching each challenge above.

solutions.title: Role-permission matrix first
solutions.body: Before wireframes, we agree on a role-permission matrix of roles, objects, actions and permission levels with your product and security teams. Role-based views then hide modules a role cannot use. In Digno's three-level performance scores, the Digno score is computed at three levels: organization, department and individual employee.

solutions.title: Dense screens that stay readable
solutions.body: The data table, filter bar, bulk actions and saved views become reusable patterns that manage data density: summary first, detail on demand. For Mass Media Co., a single dashboard now covers open tasks, sales operations, recent tasks and how work flows for each client. New modules reuse those patterns in our enterprise SaaS product design work.

solutions.title: Admin and security surfaces
solutions.body: We design the admin console a security review inspects: SSO settings, SCIM (System for Cross-domain Identity Management) user provisioning, published as RFC 7644 in September 2015, an admin audit log viewer, access reviews and session settings. Those screens hold the security review evidence a SOC 2 auditor or a buyer asks for. We design them; we do not perform or certify audits.

solutions.title: Accessible design system
solutions.body: The design system ships Figma components with design tokens that match your front-end code. WCAG 2.2 target size (success criterion 2.5.8) sets a 24 × 24 CSS pixel minimum at AA; the notes also mark contrast, focus not obscured and accessible authentication (3.3.8). Empty state, loading and error variants are components, which raises design system coverage. Those notes feed the ACR.

solutions.title: AI with review and approval
solutions.body: AI review and approval is part of the design: answers show sources and confidence cues with inline edit, regenerate and undo, and AI agents get approval steps, an activity log and an easy stop button. These patterns give risk teams evidence under the four functions of the voluntary NIST AI Risk Management Framework: Govern, Map, Measure and Manage.

solutions.title: Rollout teams accept
solutions.body: New areas ship in phases behind feature flags, with a beta group first, in-app announcements, a short tour and an optional switch back during the beta. Two or three metrics, chosen from adoption rate, task time, error rate, training time and support tickets, are agreed at kick-off and compared before and after the rollout.

cta.heading: Is enterprise UX slowing your rollout or your security review?
cta.body: If it is, book a 45-minute product review. A senior designer walks through your admin, roles and core workflow and names the three changes with the biggest effect.

benefits.title: Design next to engineering
benefits.body: As an enterprise UX design agency inside tkxel, we check each design with tkxel engineers for build effort before you see it. You get annotated Figma files, components and specs, and a designer joins your sprint reviews until the screens are live.

benefits.title: Proof on a B2B platform
benefits.body: Mass Media Co. (MMC) is a digital marketing company that now runs one business-to-business (B2B) platform. MMC's order work was spread across tools that did not talk to each other. After our Mass Media Co. B2B platform revamp, order processing efficiency rose 30% and the order processing error rate was 2+, reduced from 25%.

benefits.title: Tested with real users
benefits.body: Every flow that carries risk is tested with 5 to 8 real users before engineering starts. On enterprise software, the most useful test group mixes roles, such as an approver, an admin and an operator, not only end users.

benefits.title: Works inside your process
benefits.body: We sign a mutual non-disclosure agreement (NDA) before the first detailed call and work in your Figma, Jira or Linear workspace. All Figma files, components and research notes transfer to your company when the project ends.

process.title: Role and workflow review
process.body: We read your analytics, watch session recordings and interview 6 to 10 customers and churned users. Map the stakeholders in product, IT, security and procurement as well, because each of them can stop a rollout.
process.deliverables: Role map, workflow map, priority list

process.title: Permissions, flows and wireframes
process.body: The role-permission matrix gets signed off, then the riskiest workflow steps are redesigned first and tested as clickable wireframes before visual design starts. Include an approver and an admin among the testers.

process.title: UI and accessible design system
process.body: Final screens cover the data-dense patterns, the admin console and every AI state. They are built from Figma components with tokens and WCAG 2.2 AA annotations that your engineers reuse in every sprint.
process.deliverables: Final screens, component library, accessibility notes

process.title: Build support and rollout
process.body: Our designers join sprint reviews, run design QA on built screens and plan the beta group and phased release. Adoption metrics are compared before and after. Later, an embedded design team for long enterprise roadmaps keeps the system current.

faqs.a: Enterprise UX covers how employees and partners work in software their organization buys, such as SaaS platforms, internal tools, enterprise resource planning (ERP) and customer relationship management (CRM) systems. It differs from consumer UX in four ways: many roles share one product, the buyer is not the user, screens carry dense data and sessions last most of the workday. Teams judge it by task time and error rate rather than delight.

faqs.q: How is enterprise UX design different for AI features?
faqs.a: Enterprise UX design for AI features adds sources, human review, approval steps and an activity log, because AI output changes and can be wrong. NIST released its AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) 1.0 on January 26, 2023, as a voluntary framework, and the Generative AI Profile (NIST-AI-600-1) followed on July 26, 2024. Our AI UX design for copilots and internal AI tools applies these patterns to AI copilot UX and agents.

faqs.q: Can you design enterprise software for Section 508 and WCAG 2.2 AA?
faqs.a: Yes. We design enterprise software to WCAG 2.2 AA, which also covers the WCAG 2.0 A and AA criteria that Section 508 references. The World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) published WCAG 2.2 as a Recommendation on October 5, 2023, with 9 new success criteria over 2.1, and content that conforms to 2.2 also conforms to 2.1 and 2.0. We annotate each screen for the AA accessibility conformance level; your team or an accessibility auditor completes the ACR.

faqs.q: Do you help enterprise products pass SOC 2 security reviews?
faqs.a: Yes, on the interface side only. We design the screens a SOC 2 auditor or a buyer's security team asks to see: SSO and MFA settings, SCIM provisioning, role changes, audit logs and access reviews. The SOC 2 report itself comes from an independent CPA firm: a Type 1 report covers control design at a point in time, and a Type 2 report covers operating effectiveness over a period of time. We do not audit or certify.

faqs.q: How do you get employees to adopt a redesigned enterprise tool?
faqs.a: We ship a redesigned enterprise tool one area at a time, with the old view still available during the beta, so employees switch over step by step. Change management runs through that beta: a small group tries each new area first, and we fix issues before the full release. Put the power users who rely on shortcuts and saved views in that group. Our phased redesign of a legacy tool follows the same order.

faqs.q: How much does enterprise UX design cost?
faqs.a: Enterprise UX design with us costs $40,000–$180,000 for a full SaaS product, or $50,000–$200,000 for a phased redesign over 8–20 weeks. AI UX design runs $25,000–$90,000, and an embedded team costs $15,000–$40,000 per month. The number of user roles and platforms, research depth and design system scope set the final price. Our guide to UI UX design cost by engagement explains each price factor.
